t: Caltrans Standard Specifications: structure and how to read them
s: What the Standard Specifications are, how they are organized, and how a project manager actually uses them on an electrical contract.
x: Caltrans Standard Specifications: structure and how to read them In one sentence: the Standard Specifications are the rulebook that applies to every Caltrans contract. They tell you how work must be done, what materials are acceptable, how it is measured and how you get paid. .") What they are Caltrans publishes the Standard Specifications as one large book that is updated every few years. Every contract you bid on names the edition that applies, and that edition is part of the contract — even though it is not printed in your bid package. The Standard Specifications are generic : they are written for every highway project in the state. What makes them specific to your job is the combination with: the special provisions , which modify and add to the specs for this project, the project plans , which show what to build and where, the standard plans es , which show standard details (pull boxes, foundations, conduit installation). When these documents disagree, a defined order of precedence decides which one wins. How the book is organized The specifications are divided into divisions , and each division into numbered sections . A reference such as 86 2.05 reads as Section 86, subsection 2, paragraph 05 . Part What it covers Why it matters to an electrical PM Sections 1–9 — General provisions Definitions, bidding, award, scope, control of work, legal relations, prosecution and progress, payment Submittals, schedule, change orders, payment and claims all live here Sections 10–16 — General construction Work zone and traffic control, water pollution control, environmental stewardship, existing facilities Every freeway job: lane closures, BMPs during trenching, protecting existing equipment Earthwork, concrete, paving sections Excavation and backfill, concrete, asphalt and concrete repair Trench backfill, foundations, pull box surrounds, patching after trenching Section 86 — Electrical systems (general) Requirements common to all electrical work: conduit, pull boxes, conductors, splicing, grounding, service, foundations, testing The section you will open most often Section 87 — Electrical systems (specific) Each system: signals, lighting, detection, ramp metering, traffic monitoring, communications, fiber optics Where system specific materials and tests are defined Section numbers follow the recent editions of the book. Always confirm against the edition named in your contract. Anatomy of a section Most sections follow the same pattern. Once you know it, you can find anything quickly: 1. General — scope, definitions, submittals required, quality control. 2. Materials — what is acceptable (standards, ratings, approved products). 3. Construction — how to install it. 4. Payment — how the item is measured and paid (per linear foot, each, lump sum). For a PM, the two parts you read first are Submittals (what you must send before ordering or installing) and Payment (what you are actually paid for, and what is included in another item at no extra cost). How a PM uses them day to day Bidding: read the payment clause for each bid item so you know what is included in the price — for example, whether trenching and backfill are paid separately or included in the conduit item. Preconstruction: list every submittal the relevant sections require and build the submittal log from it. See submittals. Procurement: check the Materials subsections before you request quotes, so the supplier quotes a product that will be approved. See procurement long lead. In the field: when the crew asks "how deep?" or "what backfill?", the answer is in the Construction subsection — unless the special provisions or plans say otherwise. Testing and closeout: the required tests and documentation are listed in the sections; they become your acceptance checklist. See acceptance testing punch list. The rule that saves the most trouble Never read the Standard Specifications alone. Before relying on any clause, check whether the special provisions for your project modify it. Many

t: Project lifecycle: the twelve phases of a Caltrans electrical job
s: The order a Caltrans electrical project runs in, from design review to turnover, and what the PM does in each phase.
x: In one sentence: a job moves from paper to pipe to wire to equipment to tests, and each phase depends on the one before it. The flow Design review → RFIs → submittals → procurement → underground conduit → pull boxes → foundations → poles and cabinets → conductors and fiber → equipment → configuration → testing → Caltrans acceptance → punch list → closeout. Phase What happens PM focus 1. phase 1 preconstruction Read the contract, find conflicts, submit, order long lead items Submittals, RFIs, baseline schedule 2. phase 2 underground Survey, potholing, trenching or boring, conduit Utility conflicts, lane closures 3. phase 3 pull boxes foundations Pull boxes, vaults, cabinet and pole foundations Inspections before concrete 4. phase 4 structures Poles, cabinets, solar assemblies Deliveries arriving in order 5. phase 5 cable installation Conductors, fiber and communication cable Conduit proven clear first 6. phase 6 equipment installation Switches, routers, cameras, power equipment Approved equipment only 7. phase 7 fiber splicing Fusion splicing, termination, fiber tests Splice plan and test records 8. phase 8 network configuration IP addresses, VLANs, remote access Caltrans network requirements 9. phase 9 system testing Electrical, communication and functional tests Test reports 10. phase 10 acceptance testing Caltrans witnesses tests Scheduling with the RE 11. phase 11 punch list Fix every deficiency Closing items fast 12. phase 12 closeout As builts, certificates, warranties, final quantities Getting paid in full How procurement runs through it Procurement isn't a phase; it runs alongside all of them. Long lead equipment ordered in phase 1 has to arrive in phases 4 to 6. Late equipment is the most common reason an electrical job finishes late. See procurement long lead. Four systems, one job Everything you order supports one of four systems: civil (conduit, concrete, pull boxes), electrical (conductors, breakers, grounding), communications (fiber, cable, switches, routers) and power (utility service, or solar and batteries).

s: The protected pathway for power and communication cables: conduit types, fittings, and what a PM checks when ordering and installing it.
x: In one sentence: conduit is the empty pipe that protects every conductor and fiber on the job, and it is usually the largest quantity you install. Types The specifications name the conduit allowed for each use. In general terms: Rigid non metallic (PVC), Schedule 40 or 80: the usual choice underground. Rigid steel (galvanized): where more protection is needed, such as exposed runs, structures and some crossings. Coated rigid steel and flexible conduit for specific locations, as the specifications and plans allow. Which type goes where comes from Section 86, the special provisions and the plans. Sizes are shown on the plans or the conduit schedule. Materials ordered with it Item What it is for Elbows (22.5°, 45°, 90°) Change direction; sweep radius matters for fiber Couplings Join conduit sections Expansion fittings Let conduit move with temperature, for example on bridges Bell ends and bushings Protect cables where conduit enters a box Pull tape (mule tape) Left in the conduit to pull cable later. See pull tape tracer wire warning tape Innerduct Subdivides a conduit for fiber Sand bedding, slurry or concrete Bedding and encasement as specified Installation notes Depth, slope and bedding follow Section 86 and the plans. Keep runs clean: cap open ends during work. Prove each run clear (mandrel or swab) before cables are pulled, and when the contract requires it, before it is buried. Leave pull tape in every empty conduit. PM notes Conduit is often paid by the linear foot by size and type. Keep good daily records of footage installed; final quantities come from them. See daily reports.

s: Reading the contract, finding conflicts, submitting, ordering long-lead items and building the schedule before any field work.
x: In one sentence: phase 1 is where you win or lose the schedule: everything you don't catch on paper now becomes a delay in the field later. What happens Review the contract: special provisions, project plans and standard plans es side by side. List every piece of equipment and every test. Find conflicts: utilities, right of way, drainage, existing electrical facilities, and conflicts between documents. Send RFIs early. See rfis. Baseline CPM schedule: the schedule Caltrans approves and measures you against. First submittals: traffic control plans, the water pollution control program, shop drawings and material submittals. See submittals. Order long lead items: cabinets, batteries, routers, switches, fiber components, poles. See procurement long lead. Preconstruction meeting with the Resident Engineer: contacts, working hours, lane closure process, submittal routing. PM checklist 1. Submittal log built from the specifications. 2. Long lead list with supplier quotes and lead times. 3. RFI log started. 4. Schedule with procurement activities, not only field work. 5. Existing facility conflicts walked in the field, with photos. Goal: approvals in hand and material on order before the crew needs them.

t: Special Provisions: what they change and why they win
s: What the Special Provisions are, how they relate to the Standard Specifications, and how a project manager reads them on a Caltrans electrical job.
x: Special Provisions: what they change and why they win In one sentence: the Special Provisions are the part of the contract written for this project. They change, delete and add to the standard specifications, and when the two disagree, the Special Provisions govern. .") Where they fit Every Caltrans contract is built from the same rulebook, the Standard Specifications, plus documents written for the job. The Special Provisions are the most important of those project documents. They arrive in the bid package (in the Notice to Bidders and Special Provisions book), together with the project plans and the bid forms. Together, the Special Provisions, the Revised Standard Specifications and the Standard Specifications make up the contract specifications . You never read one without the others. What is inside Special Provisions are organized with the same section numbers as the Standard Specifications, so Section 86 of the Special Provisions talks about the same subject as Section 86 of the book. Inside, you will typically find: Replacements: a paragraph of the Standard Specifications is replaced with new wording. Additions: new paragraphs or new subsections, for work the book doesn't cover or covers differently. Deletions: a requirement of the book that doesn't apply to this job. Project specific information: working days, liquidated damages, the DBE goal, the edition of the Standard Specifications and Standard Plans that applies, and any Revised Standard Plans. Most of the text is not written from scratch. Caltrans maintains Standard Special Provisions (SSPs) , standard wording that designers pick and fill in. When no standard wording fits, the designer writes a non standard special provision (nSSP) . On electrical jobs, the nSSPs are where you usually find specific equipment: a particular cabinet, router, switch, camera or battery requirement. How a PM uses them At bid time: read Sections 86 and 87 of the Special Provisions before pricing anything. Approved products, testing requirements and payment rules often change there. For submittals: every "submit" in the Special Provisions adds a line to your submittal log, on top of what the Standard Specifications already require. See submittals. For procurement: an nSSP that names a specific product or performance requirement is a long lead warning. Ask suppliers early. See procurement long lead. In the field: when the crew's question is answered by the book, check that the Special Provisions don't say otherwise before giving the answer. Why they win The contract sets an order of precedence for when its parts disagree, and the Special Provisions sit at the top of it: they govern over the project plans, the Standard Specifications and the Standard Plans. That is why the rule "never read the Standard Specifications alone" matters so much. If the conflict is real and the order of precedence doesn't settle it, don't guess: send an RFI to the Resident Engineer and wait for a written answer. Section numbers and document names follow recent editions. Always confirm against the edition named in your contract.

s: The parts of a Caltrans traffic signal system, from the controller cabinet to the heads and push buttons, and how a job installs them.
x: In one sentence: a traffic signal is a controller in a cabinet that switches signal heads in a timed sequence, adjusted by what the detectors see. Main parts Part What it does Controller and cabinet Runs the timing; Caltrans uses standard controller and cabinet models named in the contract. See equipment cabinets Signal standards and mast arms Hold the heads over and beside the road. See foundations Signal heads Vehicle and pedestrian indications, usually LED Pedestrian push buttons Call a pedestrian phase; accessible push buttons where required Detection Tells the controller where vehicles are. See vehicle detection Emergency vehicle preemption Gives emergency vehicles a green, when specified Battery backup Keeps the signal running in a power outage. See battery backup systems Signal and interconnect cable From cabinet to heads, and to other signals or the TMC Details are on the ES standard plans es and the signal sheets of the plans. How it is built Conduit and pull boxes, foundations, standards and cabinet, cable, heads and buttons, then cabinet wiring and the turn on. Turn on A new or modified signal is turned on in a planned sequence agreed with Caltrans: timing loaded, heads checked, often with temporary traffic control and Caltrans staff present. PM notes Signal work at an existing intersection is often staged to keep the signal running. Plan temporary signals or staging. Order the controller cabinet early; it may need factory testing.

t: What a Caltrans electrical contractor does
s: The work an electrical contractor builds along California highways, who it works for, and how a job is organized.
x: In one sentence: an electrical contractor on a Caltrans job builds the power, communications and field devices that let Caltrans light, signal, watch and manage the highway. The work Most Caltrans electrical work falls into a few families of systems: Traffic signals at ramps and intersections. See traffic signals. Vehicle detection that counts and measures traffic. See vehicle detection. Highway lighting and sign lighting. See highway lighting. Ramp metering , the signals that release cars onto the freeway. See ramp metering. Traffic monitoring and ITS : cameras, changeable message signs and the stations that report to the Traffic Management Center. See cctv and video and changeable message signs. Communications that tie it all together: fiber optics, network switches and cellular routers. See fiber optic communications and network equipment. Power for all of it, from a utility service or, at remote sites, from solar panels and batteries. See service equipment and solar power and batteries. Underneath every system is the same civil work: conduit, pull boxes and foundations. That is usually most of the crew's hours. Who is who Caltrans is the owner. On each contract, a Resident Engineer (RE) runs the job for Caltrans, with inspectors in the field. The prime contractor holds the contract. On an electrical only job, the electrical contractor is often the prime; on a larger job (paving, bridges), it is usually a subcontractor to the prime. Suppliers furnish the materials and equipment, and specialty subcontractors may handle fiber splicing, boring or striping. How a job is organized Every job follows the same arc: read the contract, get submittals approved, order material, build underground, install structures and equipment, test, get Caltrans to accept it, and close out. The lifecycle overview walks through the twelve phases. The contract itself is a set of documents: the standard specifications, the special provisions, the project plans and the standard plans es. Knowing how to read them, and which one wins, is half the job. See order of precedence.

s: How to write a Request for Information that gets a fast, clear answer from the Resident Engineer.
x: In one sentence: an RFI is a written question to the engineer when the contract is unclear, contradictory, or doesn't match the field. When to write one Two documents disagree and the order of precedence doesn't settle it. A requirement is unclear or missing. The field doesn't match the plans: a utility in the way, a grade that doesn't work, an existing facility not shown. What a good RFI contains 1. A clear subject: location and topic, for example "Pull box at Sta 12+50: conflict with storm drain". 2. References: sheet numbers, specification sections, photos. 3. The problem , stated in one or two sentences. 4. A proposed solution. It speeds the answer and shows you've thought about it. 5. The impact: what is on hold, and by when you need an answer. One question per RFI. Number them and keep a log: number, date sent, subject, date answered, answer, and whether it affects cost or time. After the answer If the answer changes the work, cost or time, it may lead to a change order. Say so in writing quickly. See change orders. PM notes Send RFIs early. One sent in phase 1 costs a day; one found in the field costs a crew.

t: Order of precedence: which contract document wins
s: When the Special Provisions, plans, Standard Specifications and Standard Plans disagree, Section 5-1.02 decides which one governs. Here is the order and how to use it.
x: Order of precedence: which contract document wins In one sentence: when two parts of a Caltrans contract disagree, Section 5 1.02 of the standard specifications lists which one governs, starting with the special provisions. .") The order Section 5 1.02 ( Contract Components , in Section 5, Control of Work ) lists the parts of the contract in the order they govern when there is a discrepancy: 1. Special Provisions 2. Project plans 3. Standard Specifications (as revised by the Revised Standard Specifications) 4. Revised Standard Plans 5. Standard Plans 6. Supplemental project information The same section adds one more rule: on a drawing, written numbers and notes govern over the graphics . If a dimension is written on the plan, use it; don't scale the drawing. What it means in practice Special Provisions over everything: if the Special Provisions call for a different pull box, conductor or test than the plans or the book, follow the Special Provisions. Project plans over the book and the Standard Plans: the plans show this job. If a detail on the project plans differs from the Standard Plan it refers to, the project plan wins. Revised Standard Plans over Standard Plans: when a Standard Plan sheet has been revised since the edition you are using, the revised sheet is included with the contract and replaces it. Supplemental project information last: reports and reference material (for example, geotechnical or utility information) inform the work but don't override the contract requirements above it. When the order isn't enough The order of precedence settles conflicts between documents. It doesn't settle: a requirement that is unclear rather than contradictory, a conflict inside one document, a conflict between the documents and what you find in the field (a utility where the conduit should go, a foundation that doesn't fit). In those cases, write an RFI to the Resident Engineer, describe the conflict with sheet and section references, and propose a solution. Keep working on what isn't affected, and don't build the disputed item until you have a written answer: work done on a guess may not be paid. A quick check before you build 1. Find the requirement in the Special Provisions (same section number as the book). 2. Check the project plans and their notes. 3. Check the Standard Specifications and any Revised Standard Specifications. 4. Check the Revised Standard Plans, then the Standard Plans. 5. Still unclear? RFI. Based on Section 5 1.02 of recent editions. Always confirm against the edition named in your contract.

s: Survey and staking, potholing, then trenching or directional boring to install the conduit pathway.
x: In one sentence: phase 2 builds the empty pathway every future system will use, and it is where most surprises are found. What happens Survey and staking: mark pull boxes, poles, cabinets and conduit routes from the plans. Utility locates: call the one call center before digging, and wait for marks. Potholing: expose existing utilities where the route crosses or runs close to them. Confirm depth and owner. If a conflict appears, stop and write an RFI; it may become a change order. See change orders. Trenching or directional boring: install conduit, innerduct and any ground or tracer wire. See trenching vs boring and conduit. Backfill and restoration to the specification, then patch paving. PM focus Lane closures booked and traffic control set up as approved. Water pollution control BMPs in place before digging. Daily reports that record what was found, especially utility conflicts and delays. See daily reports. Conduit proven clear (mandrel or swab) before it is covered when the contract requires it. At the end of this phase, the pathway exists but nothing is in it.

s: Building the submittal log from the contract, preparing submittals that get approved the first time, and tracking them.
x: In one sentence: a submittal is the product data, drawings or samples you send for approval before you order or install, and nothing should be installed without it. Building the log Go through the standard specifications and the special provisions and list every "submit": material lists, product data, shop and working drawings, test plans, certificates, schedules. On electrical jobs, Sections 86 and 87 and their Special Provisions produce most of the list. For each line: specification reference, description, submitted date, response, resubmittal, approval date. A submittal that gets approved Cover sheet with the contract number, the specification section and the item. Highlight the exact model, options and ratings on the cut sheet; cross out what doesn't apply. Show compliance: point to where each requirement is met. One subject per submittal , but complete. Include the Caltrans form or format the contract or the Resident Engineer requires. Review time The specifications set how long Caltrans has to review. Build that time, and a possible resubmittal, into the schedule. See procurement long lead. PM notes Submit long lead items first, and submit them complete: a returned submittal restarts the clock.

t: The day-to-day of a GC project manager
s: What a project manager at a small electrical general contractor actually does on Caltrans jobs, day by day and phase by phase.
x: In one sentence: the field crew builds the system; the project manager makes sure every piece is approved, ordered, delivered, installed, tested, documented and paid, in the right order. A typical day Morning: check the daily reports from the foremen, answer field questions, and look at what material the crew needs this week. See daily reports. Midday: chase submittals and RFIs with the Resident Engineer, call suppliers about lead times and deliveries. See submittals and rfis. Afternoon: update the schedule, prepare change order backup, plan the next lane closures, and file paperwork Caltrans needs to pay the job. What the PM owns Area What it means in practice Contract Knowing the Special Provisions, plans and bid items better than anyone on the job Submittals Getting every material and drawing approved before it is ordered or installed Procurement Quotes, purchase orders, lead times, deliveries. See procurement long lead Schedule The baseline CPM schedule and its updates RFIs and changes Asking the right questions in writing and getting paid for extra work. See change orders Documentation Daily reports, certificates, test results, as builts Closeout Getting the system accepted and the final package delivered. See closeout package Where the time goes by phase Early in a job, most time goes to reading the contract, submittals and long lead orders. In the middle, it is coordination: material arriving on time, the crew working in the right order, field problems turned into RFIs. At the end, it is testing, the punch list and paperwork. The lifecycle overview shows how the phases connect. The habit that matters most Write things down. A phone call that changes the work isn't a change until it is in writing. An RFI answered by email is evidence. A daily report that mentions a delay is the start of a claim. Caltrans pays for what is documented.

s: The two ways conduit goes underground on a highway job, when each one is used, and the risks of each.
x: In one sentence: trenching is open and predictable; boring avoids cutting pavement and traffic but hides what is underground. Trenching An open trench is cut, conduit is laid on bedding, and the trench is backfilled and the surface restored. Best for: shoulders, unpaved areas, short runs, many conduits together. Watch: traffic control, pavement restoration, compaction, and keeping the trench safe and short. Horizontal directional drilling (boring) A drill steers a pilot bore underground, then pulls the conduit back through it. Best for: crossing roadways, ramps, driveways, waterways or landscaped areas without opening them. Watch: utilities you can't see, the depth of the bore, frac outs (drilling fluid surfacing), and a bore log to record the actual path. Choosing The plans or specifications sometimes require one method for a location. Otherwise, choose on cost, traffic impact and risk. Boring is often done by a specialty subcontractor. PM notes Pothole the utilities the bore will cross before drilling. Keep the bore logs: they become the as built depth record. If a utility conflict forces a new route, write an RFI before changing it. See rfis.

s: How Caltrans detects vehicles: inductive loops, magnetometers, video and radar, and what each needs from the contractor.
x: In one sentence: detection tells signals, ramp meters and the TMC where vehicles are and how traffic is moving. Types Type How it works Notes Inductive loops Wire loops cut into the pavement; a vehicle changes their inductance Saw cutting and sealant; sensitive to pavement work Magnetometers Small in pavement sensors that sense the vehicle's magnetic field Often wireless to a nearby receiver Video detection Cameras with software that detects vehicles in zones Aiming and zone setup matter Radar Pole mounted sensors that measure presence or speed Used for counts and speeds on freeways The contract names the type and the layout on the plans. What the contractor installs Loops or sensors, lead in cable to the cabinet, detector cards or processors in the cabinet, and the setup (sensitivity, zones). See conductors and cables. Testing Loops are tested for inductance and insulation; every detector must report correctly to the controller or the TMC. See phase 9 system testing. PM notes Coordinate loops with paving: cut loops in new pavement only when the schedule allows, and protect existing loops during other work.

s: Roadway, interchange, sign and underpass lighting: poles, luminaires, circuits and controls.
x: In one sentence: highway lighting puts light where drivers need it at night: interchanges, ramps, signs and underpasses. Main parts Part What it does Lighting standards and arms Hold the luminaires. See foundations Luminaires LED fixtures; type and distribution set by the contract Sign lighting Lights overhead guide signs when required Soffit lighting Lights underpasses and structures Circuits and service Power from the service through the lighting circuits. See service equipment Controls Photocells or controllers that switch lights on at dusk How it is built Conduit and pull boxes, foundations, poles and arms, conductors, luminaires, then circuit tests and a night check. PM notes Lighting poles near traffic may need breakaway bases; follow the details. Check voltage drop on long circuits matches the design; conductor size comes from the plans. Do a night inspection before acceptance: every luminaire lit and aimed.

s: How the wiki is organized, how articles link together, and what it is (and is not).
x: In one sentence: this wiki explains how Caltrans electrical work runs, from the contract documents to the last test, in plain language and from a contractor's side of the table. How it is organized Start here: the big picture. Read what a caltrans electrical contractor does and pm day to day first. Contract documents: the standard specifications, special provisions, project plans, standard plans es, the bid package, and the order of precedence that decides which one wins. Project lifecycle: the twelve phases of a job, in order. Start with the lifecycle overview. Shared components: what every system is built on: conduit, pull boxes, foundations, conductors, grounding, cabinets and testing. Systems: each system Caltrans installs, from traffic signals to fiber optics and solar power. PM processes: RFIs, submittals, procurement, daily reports, change orders, acceptance and closeout. Glossary: terms and abbreviations. Underlined terms in an article link there. Reading an article Each article starts with a one sentence summary, then explains what the thing is, how it is used on a job, and what a project manager should watch for. Most end with a Common mistakes box: what goes wrong in practice and what Caltrans checks. The sidebar shows the article's sections, linked articles and tags. What this wiki is not It is not Caltrans guidance and not a contract interpretation. Section numbers and requirements change between editions, and every contract's Special Provisions change the rules for that job. Always check the documents of your own contract, and ask the Resident Engineer in writing when something is unclear. Search Use the search box at the top of every page to find an article or a term.

s: Setting pull boxes and vaults on the conduit runs, and building cabinet, pole and sign foundations.
x: In one sentence: phase 3 creates the access points and the bases that everything above ground will stand on. Pull boxes Pull boxes and vaults are set where the conduit runs change direction, at devices, and at intervals along long runs, as shown on the plans. They include communication and fiber pull boxes. See pull boxes. Foundations Cast in place foundations for cabinets, signal and lighting poles, sign structures, camera poles and solar assemblies. Each one needs the right anchor bolts set to template, conduit stubs in the right place and a ground rod or grounding as detailed. See foundations. Inspection, then concrete Caltrans inspects the excavation, reinforcement, anchor bolts and conduit before the pour. Concrete must cure before a pole or cabinet is loaded on it. Keep the concrete delivery tickets; they are part of the closeout record. PM focus Anchor bolt templates and bolts ordered with the poles; they're often needed first. Inspection requested in time for the pour. Correct number and size of conduit stubs: missing one means breaking concrete later.

s: Getting quotes, issuing purchase orders and tracking long-lead equipment so it arrives when the crew needs it.
x: In one sentence: procurement turns approved submittals into material on site at the right time, and long lead items are where schedules slip. Typical long lead items on electrical jobs Controller and equipment cabinets. Poles, mast arms and anchor bolts. Changeable message signs and cameras. Batteries, especially lithium batteries with shipping rules. Network equipment: switches, routers, specific SFP modules. Fiber cable in specific fiber counts. The cycle 1. Quote: send suppliers the specification and plan references, not just a part number. 2. Submit the quoted product. See submittals. 3. Purchase order as soon as it is approved, or earlier with the supplier's agreement for very long lead times. 4. Track fabrication and shipping dates every week. 5. Receive: check the delivery against the PO and the approved submittal; note damage on the ticket. 6. Store safely, and keep certificates and manuals for closeout. Ordering bulk material For conduit, pull boxes, conductors and fittings, ask the foremen what is left before reordering, and keep a running takeoff against what is installed. See daily reports. PM notes Put procurement in the schedule with real lead times. A missing cabinet stops a system as surely as a missing crew.

t: Project plans: sheet types, legends and electrical sheets
s: How a set of Caltrans project plans is organized, how to find the electrical sheets, and how a PM reads them for takeoffs and field work.
x: In one sentence: the project plans show what to build on this job and where; the electrical sheets are the ones your crew will live in. How a plan set is organized A Caltrans plan set is a stack of sheets grouped by discipline. A typical order is: title sheet and location map, typical cross sections, layouts, construction details, stage construction and traffic handling, drainage, utilities, then the specialty sheets such as electrical , signs and striping, and structures. Each sheet has a title block with the sheet number, the total number of sheets, the contract number and the engineer's stamp. The electrical sheets Electrical sheets usually include: Electrical legend and abbreviations: the symbols for pull boxes, conduit, poles, cabinets and devices. Read it first; symbols differ between districts and designers. Plan sheets (layouts): where each pull box, conduit run, pole and cabinet goes, with stationing and offsets. Schedules and details: conductor and conduit schedules, pole and equipment schedules, wiring diagrams, cabinet details and system block diagrams. Communication sheets on ITS jobs: fiber routes, splice diagrams and network diagrams. The plans refer to standard details by Standard Plan number instead of drawing them. See standard plans es. How a PM uses them Takeoff: count devices and measure conduit and conductor runs to check the bid quantities. Note what is paid as a bid item and what is included in another item. Submittals and procurement: the schedules name the equipment to submit and order. See submittals. Field layout: stationing and offsets tell the crew where to stake. Written dimensions govern over scaling the drawing. See order of precedence. As builts: mark changes on a set of plans as the work happens; it becomes the as built record at closeout. See closeout package. When the plans disagree If the plans conflict with the special provisions, the Special Provisions govern. If the plans conflict with the field (a utility, a slope, a sign in the way), write an RFI. See rfis.

s: Underground access points along conduit runs: sizes, covers, extensions and grounding, and what to check before setting them.
x: In one sentence: a pull box is the buried box with a lid where crews pull, splice and later service the cables. What they are for Pull boxes break long conduit runs into lengths that can be pulled, give access at devices, poles and cabinets, and hold slack and splices. Larger vaults hold fiber splice closures and many conduits. Types and sizes Caltrans pull boxes come in standard numbered sizes, with covers and details shown on the ES Standard Plans. See standard plans es. The project plans show which size goes where. Communication and fiber pull boxes may be larger or specified in the special provisions. Item What it is for Concrete or polymer concrete box The body; polymer concrete is lighter and corrosion resistant Cover (lid) Secures the opening; marking shows the system (for example, electrical or communications) Extension Adds depth where needed Ground rod and bonding Grounds metal covers and equipment as detailed. See grounding and bonding Drain rock Lets water drain under the box Installation notes Set to grade, on drain rock, with conduit entering as detailed. Use traffic rated boxes and covers where vehicles can drive over them. Keep boxes clear of dirt; clean them before pulling cable and before acceptance. PM notes Pull boxes are often among the first materials needed. Order them with the conduit, and check the plan count against the bid item list.

s: What goes in a daily report on a Caltrans job and why it is the most important record you keep.
x: In one sentence: the daily report is the job's diary: it proves what was done, with whom, and what got in the way. .") What to record each day Date, contract and locations worked. Crew: names, classifications and hours. Equipment used. Work performed and quantities installed (feet of conduit, boxes set, foundations poured). Materials received. Subcontractors on site. Inspections and who from Caltrans was present. Delays and problems: weather, utility conflicts, waiting on answers, lane closure cancellations. Safety meeting held and topics. Photos. Why it matters Payment: quantities in daily reports support final quantities. Change orders and claims: a delay that isn't in the daily report is very hard to prove later. See change orders. Timesheets and certified payroll follow from the labor recorded. PM notes Make it easy for foremen to file the same day, from the field, with photos. Review them daily and follow up on anything that sounds like a change.

s: Cast-in-place foundations that support poles, cabinets and structures: anchor bolts, reinforcement, conduit stubs and inspection.
x: In one sentence: a foundation is the concrete base a pole or cabinet bolts onto, and it has to be right the first time. Types Pole foundations for signal and lighting standards, CCTV and communication poles: usually drilled, reinforced concrete piles. Cabinet foundations: a pad with conduit stubs coming up under the cabinet. Sign and solar foundations as detailed on the plans. Dimensions and reinforcement come from the standard plans es and the project plans. Materials Item What it is for Anchor bolts and templates Hold the pole or cabinet; the template sets the bolt pattern Rebar Reinforces the concrete Forms or sonotubes Shape the foundation above ground Concrete The foundation itself; keep the tickets Ground rod and conductor Grounding as detailed. See grounding and bonding Conduit stubs Bring the conduits up into the pole or cabinet Inspection The inspector checks the excavation, reinforcement, bolt pattern, conduit stubs and grounding before the pour. Concrete must cure before loading. See phase 3 pull boxes foundations. PM notes Anchor bolts often come with the poles but are needed weeks earlier. Order them first.

s: Installing poles, camera and communication poles, solar assemblies and equipment cabinets.
x: In one sentence: in phase 4 the job becomes visible: poles stand up and cabinets go on their foundations. What happens Poles: signal and lighting standards, mast arms, CCTV poles and communication poles, set on cured foundations and plumbed. Solar assemblies: panel mounts and battery enclosures at sites without utility power. See solar power and batteries. Equipment cabinets: set on foundations, sealed and grounded. See equipment cabinets. PM focus Deliveries in order: poles and cabinets are long lead items and need storage or same day setting. Lifting plans and lane closures for setting poles near traffic. Damage on arrival: inspect finishes and record any damage before signing the delivery ticket. Shop drawing match: height, arm length and bolt pattern match the approved submittal. After this phase, the structures exist, but they aren't wired.

s: The signals that release vehicles onto the freeway at a controlled rate: cabinet, signals, detection and communication.
x: In one sentence: a ramp meter is a small signal on an on ramp that lets cars onto the freeway one or two at a time, timed from what the detectors see. Main parts Part What it does Ramp meter controller and cabinet Runs the metering rate. See equipment cabinets Meter signal heads Red/green signals at the stop line Detection Demand, passage, queue and mainline detectors. See vehicle detection Signs Advance warning signs, sometimes with flashers Communication Link to the TMC for monitoring and rate changes. See network equipment How it works Detectors on the ramp and freeway tell the controller how much traffic there is. The controller sets the rate, and the TMC can monitor and change it remotely. PM notes Detector layout and lane numbering must match the plans exactly; the TMC reads them by number. Plan the turn on with Caltrans operations staff.

s: What the Caltrans Standard Plans are, what the ES electrical sheets cover, and how revised standard plans fit in.
x: In one sentence: the Standard Plans are Caltrans's book of standard drawings, and the ES sheets are the electrical details your project plans point to instead of drawing them again. What they are Caltrans publishes a set of Standard Plans alongside the standard specifications. Each sheet shows a standard detail used on many projects. The project plans reference a Standard Plan by its number, and that detail becomes part of the contract. Standard Plans are grouped by letter prefix by subject. The ES sheets cover electrical systems . What the ES sheets cover The ES series typically includes: Symbols and abbreviations used on electrical plans. Pull boxes: sizes, covers, installation and grounding. See pull boxes. Conduit installation details. See conduit. Foundations for signal, lighting and sign poles and for cabinets. See foundations. Poles, mast arms and luminaire arms for signals and lighting. Signal heads, mountings and detector loops. See traffic signals and vehicle detection. Service equipment and cabinet details. See service equipment and equipment cabinets. Sheet numbers and contents change between editions, so look up the exact sheet in the edition your contract names. Revised Standard Plans When a Standard Plan sheet changes after the edition was published, Caltrans issues a Revised Standard Plan (RSP) . RSPs that apply are included with the contract, and they govern over the original sheet. See order of precedence. How a PM uses them During takeoff: a single symbol on the plans may stand for a whole Standard Plan detail (the box, the cover, the grounding, the extension). Price the detail, not just the symbol. For submittals: standard details still need the materials submitted that meet them. In the field: give the crew the Standard Plan sheet with the project plan sheet. Many field questions are answered on the ES sheet. If the project plans show something different from the Standard Plan they reference, the project plans govern.

s: Traffic cameras that let the TMC watch the highway: cameras, poles, encoders and the network behind them.
x: In one sentence: CCTV cameras let the Traffic Management Center see incidents and conditions live and react. Main parts Part What it does Camera (PTZ or fixed) Pan tilt zoom cameras are remotely controlled; fixed cameras watch one view CCTV pole and mount Raises the camera for a clear view. See foundations Video encoder (if needed) Converts video to network streams for older or analog cameras Network equipment Switch, fiber or cellular router back to the TMC. See network equipment Surge protection On power and data at the pole. See surge protection Power Utility service or solar. See solar power and batteries Setup Cameras get IP addresses and settings from Caltrans, are added to the TMC's video system, and are aimed and given preset views. Testing Caltrans checks it can see the stream, control pan tilt zoom, and recall presets. See phase 9 system testing. PM notes Confirm camera model, video format and TMC software compatibility at submittal time. A camera the TMC can't read is a failed test.

s: How extra or changed work becomes a Contract Change Order, and how to document it so you get paid.
x: In one sentence: when the work changes, a Contract Change Order (CCO) changes the contract so you are paid for it. Where changes come from Differing conditions: potholing finds a utility where the conduit should go; the ground isn't what was expected. Caltrans changes: a device moves, equipment is added, a design changes. Document problems: an RFI answer that adds work. See rfis. How it works 1. Notify in writing promptly when you believe work is extra or changed. The specifications set notice requirements; missing them can cost the right to be paid. 2. Document: photos, daily reports, potholing results, RFI and answer. 3. Price: agreed lump sum, unit prices, or force account (tracked labor, equipment and materials). 4. CCO issued by Caltrans, signed by both sides, with any time extension. Force account When the price can't be agreed in advance, the work is paid on actual labor, equipment and materials plus markups. Daily force account records must be signed by the inspector each day. PM notes Keep a change log: description, date notified, status, value, time impact. Review it in every weekly meeting with the Resident Engineer.

s: Power conductors, grounding conductors, and signal, detector and communication cables: what each is for and how they are installed.
x: In one sentence: conductors carry power, and cables carry signals and data; both are pulled through the conduit and terminated in cabinets and devices. Power conductors Copper conductors sized and insulated as the specifications and conductor schedule require, from the service to the cabinets and devices. Color coding follows the specifications. Grounding conductors Bare or insulated conductors that bond equipment, poles and boxes to the grounding system. See grounding and bonding. Signal and communication cables Signal cable (multi conductor) from the controller cabinet to signal heads. See traffic signals. Detector lead in cable from loops or sensors to the cabinet. See vehicle detection. CAT6 and control cables for network devices. Fiber optic cable. See fiber optic communications. Installation notes Pull only after the conduit is proven clear. See phase 5 cable installation. Respect pulling tension and bend radius; use lubricant made for cable. Splice only where allowed, with the splice method specified. Label at both ends and in pull boxes. See labeling and identification. Test insulation before energizing. See electrical testing. PM notes Keep the reel tags and certifications for the submittal and closeout records.

s: Pulling power conductors, fiber optic cable and communication cable through the finished conduit system.
x: In one sentence: phase 5 fills the pathway: conductors, fiber and communication cable are pulled from box to box. Before pulling Prove the conduit is continuous and clear. A blocked run found during a pull costs a lot more than one found with a mandrel. What is pulled Power: service conductors, branch circuits and grounding conductors. See conductors and cables. Fiber optic cable: backbone and distribution fiber, with slack loops left at pull boxes as specified. See fiber optic communications. Communication and control cable: CAT6, detector lead in, signal and control cables. Good practice Don't exceed the cable's pulling tension or bend radius, especially for fiber. Label each cable at both ends and in pull boxes as it is pulled. See labeling and identification. Keep the reel tags: they hold the cable data for submittals and records. At the end of this phase, everything is connected physically but nothing is terminated.

t: The bid package: bid items, quantities and the Bid Item List
s: What comes in a Caltrans bid package, how bid items and quantities work, and what a PM checks before pricing an electrical job.
x: In one sentence: the bid package is everything you need to price the job: the plans, the Special Provisions, the bid forms and the list of bid items you will be paid on. What is in it A Caltrans bid package usually contains: Notice to Bidders and Special Provisions: the bid date, working days, liquidated damages, the DBE goal, and the special provisions. Project plans. See project plans. Bid book: the bid forms and certifications, including the Bid Item List . Information handout or supplemental information when available: reports and reference material. Addenda issued before the bid date. Each one must be acknowledged. The standard specifications and standard plans es are part of the contract by reference; they aren't printed in the package. Bid items The Bid Item List is the list of things Caltrans pays for, each with an item number, a description, a unit (each, linear foot, lump sum) and an estimated quantity. You enter a unit price for each item. Two rules matter most: Payment follows the contract, not your cost. The payment clause in the specifications says what each item includes. Work that isn't a separate item is included in other items. Quantities are estimates for unit price items. You are paid for the quantity actually installed and measured; lump sum items are paid as a whole. On electrical jobs, systems are often paid as lump sum (for example, a signal and lighting system at one location), with some items such as conduit or fiber paid by the foot. What a PM checks before pricing 1. Read Sections 86 and 87 of the Special Provisions for equipment, testing and payment changes. 2. Do your own takeoff from the plans and compare it with the Bid Item List. 3. Mark long lead equipment and get supplier quotes early. See procurement long lead. 4. Check working days, lane closure restrictions and night work: they drive labor cost. 5. Note anything unclear and ask before the bid date through the bidders' inquiry process.

t: Caltrans acceptance testing and the punch list
s: Preparing for Caltrans witness tests, handling the punch list, and getting the system accepted.
x: In one sentence: acceptance is when Caltrans confirms the system works and is documented; the punch list is what stands between you and it. Before the witness test Your own tests are done and passed. See phase 9 system testing. Test reports are ready in the required format, with calibration certificates. The network is configured and devices report to the TMC. Cabinets are clean, labeled and have prints inside. During the test The Resident Engineer and inspectors, sometimes with district electrical or TMC staff, watch the tests and inspect the work. Have the crew, the fiber or network subcontractor, and test equipment on site. The punch list Common findings: labeling, missing documentation, grounding corrections, network configuration. Track every item to closure with photos. See phase 11 punch list. Acceptance Once the punch list is closed and the documents are delivered, Caltrans accepts the work (for a system or the whole contract) and maintenance responsibility passes to Caltrans. See closeout package.

s: Electronic signs that show messages sent from the TMC: the sign, its structure, controller and communication.
x: In one sentence: a changeable message sign (CMS) shows drivers messages the TMC sends: incidents, travel times, closures. Main parts Part What it does Sign housing and display LED display in a walk in or front access housing Sign structure Overhead or roadside structure and foundation, often by others Sign controller and cabinet Receives messages and runs the display. See equipment cabinets Communication Fiber or cellular link to the TMC. See network equipment Power Service with enough capacity for the display. See service equipment Testing Caltrans checks every pixel or module, brightness control, and that the TMC can post and clear messages. PM notes A CMS is a long lead item and heavy: plan delivery, lifting and lane closures together. Confirm the controller's protocol matches the TMC software at submittal time.

s: Connecting equipment, poles, boxes and cabinets to earth and to each other so faults clear and people stay safe.
x: In one sentence: grounding gives fault current and lightning a safe path to earth; bonding ties all the metal together so nothing becomes energized. What gets grounded and bonded Service equipment and cabinets, through ground rods and a ground bar. Metal poles, through their foundations. Metal pull box covers and conduit. Equipment inside cabinets, to the cabinet ground bar. Surge protection devices. See surge protection. Materials Item What it is for Ground rods Connect the system to earth Grounding and bonding conductors Tie metal parts together Ground bars Common point in a cabinet Clamps and connectors Approved connections, sometimes exothermic welds Testing Ground resistance is measured and must meet the value in the specifications. See electrical testing. PM notes Grounding is one of the most common acceptance findings. Have the crew photograph connections before they are buried or covered. See phase 10 acceptance testing.

s: Installing the electronics: power supplies, switches, routers, surge protection, batteries and field devices.
x: In one sentence: phase 6 puts the approved equipment in the cabinets and on the poles. Inside the cabinet Power supplies, surge protection, terminal blocks, Ethernet and fiber switches, routers, patch panels, and UPS or battery backup systems. See equipment cabinets, network equipment and surge protection. Power at remote sites Solar charge controllers, batteries and PV panels. See solar power and batteries. Field devices Cameras, detection equipment, network radios, sensors and signs. See cctv and video and vehicle detection. PM focus Install only what was approved in the submittal: model numbers must match. Record serial numbers as the equipment is installed; Caltrans will ask for them. Keep the manuals and warranty papers from every box; they go in the closeout package. See closeout package.

s: Everything Caltrans needs at the end of a job: as-builts, certifications, test results, warranties, manuals and final records.
x: In one sentence: the closeout package is the proof of what you built, and the job isn't finished until it is delivered and accepted. Checklist Document Notes As built plans Every change marked, with locations and depths Fiber splice diagrams Matching the field and the labels Test results Electrical, fiber and functional tests Material certifications Certificates of compliance for materials that need them Battery certifications Model, install date, warranty Concrete tickets For foundations and encasements Warranty documents With start dates Equipment manuals One set per device type, or as the contract requires Configuration files Final switch, router and device settings Serial number list By location Final CPM schedule Updated to actual dates Acceptance records Punch list closed, sign offs Final quantities Agree on the final measured quantity of every unit price item. Daily reports and measurements support them. See daily reports. PM notes Build the package from day one. File certificates with each submittal, tests as they are run, as builts as changes happen. See phase 12 closeout.

s: Fiber optic cable, splicing, termination and testing: the backbone that connects field devices to the TMC.
x: In one sentence: fiber carries data from cameras, signs, detectors and controllers back to the Traffic Management Center. Main parts Item What it is for Fiber optic cable Backbone and distribution cables, single mode, with the fiber count on the plans Innerduct Extra protection and organization inside conduit. See conduit Splice closures Protect splices in vaults and pull boxes Splice trays Hold and organize individual splices Patch panels Terminate fibers in cabinets Fiber jumpers Connect patch panels to equipment Labels Identify every fiber and port. See labeling and identification Installation Pull with tension control, leave slack loops where specified, splice by fusion, terminate in patch panels, and follow the splice diagram on the plans. See phase 7 fiber splicing. Testing OTDR: shows each event (splice, connector, break) along the fiber and its loss. Insertion loss with a power meter and light source: the total loss of each link. The contract sets wavelengths, directions and pass limits. Clean and inspect every connector before testing. PM notes Fiber work is often subcontracted. Agree on the splice plan, the test report format and the as built splice diagram before work starts.

s: Fusion splicing, splice closures and trays, termination at patch panels, and documenting losses.
x: In one sentence: phase 7 turns pulled fiber into working links, and the test records from it are what prove the links work. What happens Fusion splicing fiber to fiber in splice closures in vaults or pull boxes, and at the cabinets. Splice trays organize the splices; every fiber goes to a known position. Termination at patch panels in the cabinets, with connectors on the field side and jumpers to the equipment. Splice records: which fiber goes where, following the splice diagram on the plans. Testing OTDR traces show each splice and connector along the fiber and its loss. Power meter (insertion loss) tests measure the total loss end to end. The contract sets which tests, at which wavelengths, in which directions, and the loss limits. See fiber optic communications. The question this phase answers: is there continuity from the field device back to the TMC? PM focus Fiber splicing is often a specialty subcontractor. Agree early on the test format Caltrans wants and on who produces the as built splice diagram.

s: How power gets from the utility to the job: the service point, meter, disconnects and breakers, and the utility coordination it takes.
x: In one sentence: the service is where the utility's power becomes Caltrans's power, and getting it energized is often on the critical path. What it includes Item What it is for Service enclosure or pedestal Houses the meter, main disconnect and breakers Meter (when required) Measures energy for the utility bill Main disconnect and breakers Isolate and protect circuits Service conductors From the utility point of connection to the enclosure Grounding Ground rods and bonding at the service. See grounding and bonding Details are on the standard plans es and the project plans. Utility coordination The utility (for example, the local power company) decides the point of connection and schedules the connection. That usually takes an application, a service request from the agency, and inspection. Lead times can be long. PM notes Start the service request in phase 1; ask the Resident Engineer who files it on this contract. Plan temporary power or a generator if equipment must run before the service is energized. Sites with no practical utility service use solar. See solar power and batteries.

s: The field cabinets that house controllers, network equipment and power: types, accessories, and what Caltrans checks.
x: In one sentence: the cabinet is the field office of every system: it holds the electronics, protects them from weather and intruders, and is where Caltrans technicians will work. What goes inside Controllers (signals, ramp meters), power supplies, surge protection, terminal blocks, switches, routers, patch panels and battery backup, depending on the system. See traffic signals, ramp metering and network equipment. Types Caltrans uses standard cabinet models for signals and ramp meters, and specified cabinets for communication hubs and ITS sites. The model is named in the plans or special provisions. Cabinets are often furnished pre wired by a manufacturer and may need factory testing before delivery. Accessory What it is for Cabinet base or riser Interface with the foundation Door switch Alarms when the cabinet is opened Fans, vents and thermostat Keep electronics cool Heater Prevents condensation Lighting and convenience outlet For technicians Surge protection Protects the electronics. See surge protection PM notes Cabinets are long lead items. Submit early. See procurement long lead. Check the approved wiring diagram against the cabinet on delivery. Keep the cabinet wiring prints inside the cabinet at turnover.

t: Network equipment: switches, routers, SFPs and cellular
s: The equipment that puts field devices on the Caltrans network: switches, routers, SFP modules, antennas and patch cords.
x: In one sentence: network equipment lets every device in the field talk to the TMC, over fiber or cellular. Main parts Item What it is for Ethernet switches Connect devices in the cabinet; managed, industrial rated Fiber switches Connect the cabinet to the fiber network SFP modules Plug in transceivers that connect a switch port to fiber Cellular routers Wireless link to the network where there is no fiber Antennas Cellular signal for the router Patch cords and CAT6 Connect equipment in the cabinet and to nearby devices The models are usually named or specified in the special provisions; the plans include a network diagram. Configuration IP addresses, VLANs, management access and security settings from Caltrans's network plan. See phase 8 network configuration. PM notes Match SFPs to the fiber type, wavelength and distance; the wrong SFP is a common cause of a dead link. Cellular routers need carrier service set up; confirm who provides the SIM and data plan. Save every final configuration file for the closeout package. See closeout package.

s: Programming switches and routers, assigning IP addresses and VLANs, and proving remote access.
x: In one sentence: in phase 8 the hardware is programmed so that each device can talk to Caltrans. What is configured Switches (managed industrial Ethernet or fiber switches): ports, VLANs, management addresses. Cellular routers at sites without fiber: carrier, VPN or tunnel settings Caltrans specifies. IP addresses for every device, from the plan Caltrans provides. Device settings: cameras, detectors, signs and controllers set up to report to the TMC. What is verified Communication paths from each device to the TMC. Remote access works the way Caltrans requires. Security settings: default passwords changed, unused ports disabled, firmware as approved. PM focus Get the IP plan and network requirements from Caltrans early: they are often the last piece to arrive. Many projects are physically finished but stay open until networking works. See network equipment.

s: The contractor's own electrical, communication and functional tests before Caltrans witnesses anything.
x: In one sentence: phase 9 is your own test run: find and fix the problems before Caltrans comes to watch. Electrical tests Voltage, insulation resistance, continuity, grounding, battery operation and solar charging. See electrical testing. Communication tests Fiber performance, router and switch communication, and each device reachable on the network. Functional tests Test the system the way Caltrans will use it: Can Caltrans see the camera? Can it reach the switch and the field cabinet? Do the alarms (door open, power fail) reach the TMC? Does the signal, sign or meter do what the plans say? PM focus Write every result down in the format of the final test report. A test you can't show didn't happen. Schedule the Caltrans witness tests only after your own tests pass. See acceptance testing punch list.

s: Powering remote sites without utility power: panels, charge controllers, batteries and sizing.
x: In one sentence: where there is no practical utility service, solar panels charge batteries that run the site day and night. Main parts Item What it is for Solar panels Generate electricity Panel mounts Support and tilt the panels on the pole or structure Charge controller Regulates battery charging and protects the batteries Batteries (often LiFePO4) Store energy for night and cloudy days Battery enclosure and trays Hold and protect the batteries Battery cables and DC disconnect Connect the bank; let crews isolate it safely Sizing The design sets panel and battery capacity from the load (camera, radio, router) and the days of autonomy required. Don't substitute smaller equipment. Batteries Lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) batteries are common for their life and safety, and some contracts require them. They are long lead items with shipping rules for lithium batteries. See procurement long lead. Testing Caltrans may check charging, battery voltage, and that the site runs on battery alone. See phase 9 system testing.

s: Devices that protect field electronics from lightning and power surges, and where they go.
x: In one sentence: surge protection diverts voltage spikes to ground before they reach the electronics. Where it goes On the power service and the cabinet's main power input. On signal and data lines that leave the cabinet: detector lead ins, Ethernet to pole mounted devices, antenna feeds. On equipment as the specifications or the manufacturer require. How it works A surge protective device connects between the line and ground. It only works if the grounding is good, so it depends on grounding and bonding. PM notes Submit the devices specified for each location; they differ by voltage and signal type. Many devices have a status indicator. Check that they are healthy before acceptance.

s: Systems that keep traffic signals and field equipment running during power outages.
x: In one sentence: a battery backup system (BBS) keeps a signal or cabinet running for a time when utility power fails. Main parts Item What it is for Inverter and charger Switches to battery power and recharges afterward Batteries Stored energy, sized for the required run time Transfer switch / bypass Lets maintenance bypass the system Enclosure or cabinet space Houses the system, sometimes beside the controller cabinet Alarms Report power failure and battery status How it works When utility power drops, the system transfers to battery. Depending on the specification, a signal may run normally for a time, then switch to flashing operation to stretch the battery. Testing Pull the utility power and confirm the transfer, run time and alarms. PM notes Check battery shipping and storage rules, and record the battery install date; batteries have a service life and warranty that start then.

s: Caltrans witnesses the tests, reviews the documents and produces the punch list.
x: In one sentence: in phase 10 Caltrans checks that what you built works and is documented, before it takes the system over. What you provide Test reports, fiber test results, material certifications, as builts and warranty information. What Caltrans does The Resident Engineer and electrical inspectors witness the tests, sometimes with the district's electrical maintenance or TMC staff, and produce a list of deficiencies: the punch list. Common findings Labeling issues. Missing documentation. Grounding corrections. Network configuration corrections. PM focus Book the witness tests with enough notice, have the crew and any subcontractors on site, and bring the test reports printed. See acceptance testing punch list.

t: Pull tape, tracer wire and warning tape
s: The small items that make conduit usable and findable later: pull tape, tracer wire and buried warning tape.
x: In one sentence: these cheap items decide whether the next crew can use and find your conduit years from now. Item What it is for Pull tape (mule tape) Left inside conduit to pull cable later; often marked in feet Tracer wire Lets locators find non metallic conduit and fiber from the surface Warning tape Buried above the conduit to warn the next excavator Notes Leave pull tape in every empty or spare conduit, tied off at both ends. Make tracer wire continuous, with access points in pull boxes, and test it. Place warning tape at the depth the specifications or plans show. These are rarely paid as separate items, so they are easy to forget. They are also easy for an inspector to check.

s: The tests that prove an electrical installation is safe and complete: continuity, insulation resistance, ground resistance and functional tests.
x: In one sentence: testing proves the wiring is right before it is energized, and the test records prove it to Caltrans. Common tests Test What it proves Continuity Each conductor runs where it should, without breaks Insulation resistance Insulation is not damaged; no path to ground Ground resistance The grounding system meets the required value. See grounding and bonding Voltage and polarity Correct supply at each panel and device Functional test The system does what it is meant to do The tests required, how they are done and the pass values are in the specifications and special provisions. Test equipment Multimeters, insulation testers and ground resistance testers. Keep calibration certificates; Caltrans may ask for them. Fiber has its own tests. See fiber optic communications. PM notes Record results in the format of the final test report as you go. See phase 9 system testing and acceptance testing punch list.

s: Fixing every deficiency Caltrans found, and proving each one is fixed.
x: In one sentence: the punch list is the last quality check before turnover: close every item and get each one signed off. Typical items Missing or wrong labels. Damaged equipment or finishes. Documentation updates. Final adjustments: aiming cameras, timing, settings. How to run it 1. Turn the list into a tracker: item, location, who fixes it, date fixed, date Caltrans accepted. 2. Group items by location so the crew can fix them in one trip and one lane closure. 3. Photograph each fix. 4. Send the updated list to the Resident Engineer and ask for sign off. The job isn't accepted until the punch list is closed. See acceptance testing punch list.

s: Labels on conductors, cables, fibers, pull boxes and equipment, and why they are one of the most common punch-list items.
x: In one sentence: labels let Caltrans maintenance find and fix things for the next twenty years. What gets labeled Conductors and cables at both ends and in every pull box. Fibers, splice trays and patch panel ports , matching the splice diagram. Pull box covers with the system marking. Cabinets, breakers and equipment , matching the as builts. Good practice Use the label format and material the specifications call for: durable, readable, weather proof. Label as you pull and terminate, not at the end. Keep labels consistent with the plans, the splice diagram and the as builts. Why it matters Labeling is one of the most frequent findings in phase 10 acceptance testing. Fixing labels after the fact means reopening boxes and cabinets, often with a lane closure.

s: Delivering as-builts, certificates, test results and warranties, reconciling final quantities, and turning the system over.
x: In one sentence: closeout turns a finished system into an accepted contract and the final payment. Documentation As built plans, material certifications, fiber splice diagrams, test results, warranty packages, equipment manuals and configuration files. See closeout package. Administrative Final quantity reconciliation: agree with Caltrans on the measured quantity of every unit price item. Final schedule update. Final reports and any remaining certified payroll or compliance documents. Change orders all executed. See change orders. Turnover The system is transferred to Caltrans operations and maintenance. After acceptance, the warranty period starts. PM focus Start building the closeout package on day one: certificates with submittals, test results as they are run, as builts as changes happen. Closeout is slow when it starts at the end.

s: Plans marked with what was actually built, including changes, locations and depths.
x: As-built  Plans marked with what was actually built, including changes, locations and depths. As-builts

s: Keeps a traffic signal or cabinet running for a time during a power outage.
x: BBS Battery Backup System Keeps a traffic signal or cabinet running for a time during a power outage.

s: A measure that keeps sediment and pollutants out of storm drains during construction, such as fiber rolls, inlet protection or covering stoc
x: BMP Best Management Practice A measure that keeps sediment and pollutants out of storm drains during construction, such as fiber rolls, inlet protection or covering stockpiles.

s: A written change to the contract, issued by Caltrans, that adjusts the work, the price or the time.
x: CCO Contract Change Order A written change to the contract, issued by Caltrans, that adjusts the work, the price or the time.

s: Traffic cameras installed along the highway so the operations center can watch conditions live.
x: CCTV Closed-Circuit Television Traffic cameras installed along the highway so the operations center can watch conditions live.

s: An electronic sign over or beside the road that shows messages sent from the operations center.
x: CMS Changeable Message Sign An electronic sign over or beside the road that shows messages sent from the operations center.

s: Protective pipe that carries conductors and cables, usually buried.
x: Conduit  Protective pipe that carries conductors and cables, usually buried.

t: CPM schedule — Critical Path Method schedule
s: The project schedule that links activities in sequence and shows which ones control the finish date.
x: CPM schedule Critical Path Method schedule The project schedule that links activities in sequence and shows which ones control the finish date.

s: A certified small business; many Caltrans contracts set a DBE participation goal.
x: DBE Disadvantaged Business Enterprise A certified small business; many Caltrans contracts set a DBE participation goal.

s: Payment for changed work based on actual labor, equipment and materials plus markups, recorded daily and signed by the inspector.
x: Force account  Payment for changed work based on actual labor, equipment and materials plus markups, recorded daily and signed by the inspector.

s: Installing conduit underground by steering a drill, without an open trench.
x: HDD Horizontal Directional Drilling Installing conduit underground by steering a drill, without an open trench. Directional boring

s: Smaller duct installed inside a conduit to organize and protect fiber.
